citation: Salmoni AW, Schmidt RA, Walter CB (1984) Knowledge of results and motor learning: a review and critical reappraisal. Psychol Bull 95(3):355-386; together with Sigrist R, Rauter G, Riener R, Wolf P (2013) Augmented visual, auditory, haptic, and multimodal feedback in motor learning: a review. Psychon Bull Rev 20(1):21-53
task_or_setup: Narrative reviews of augmented feedback (knowledge of results; concurrent/terminal; visual, auditory, haptic, multimodal) and motor learning; source of the 'guidance hypothesis'
participants_or_bench: n/a (reviews)
comparator: Performance while feedback/guidance is present vs. unassisted retention/transfer
key_quantitative_findings: No effect sizes extracted. Guidance hypothesis as restated in accessed secondary sources: augmented feedback that guides is beneficial when used to reduce error but detrimental when relied upon (Winstein et al. 1994 abstract, citing Schmidt 1991); physically guiding a movement 'may actually decrease motor learning for some tasks' because it changes task dynamics so 'the task learned is not the target task' (Marchal-Crespo & Reinkensmeyer 2009). Sigrist et al. abstract: most prior studies used simple/artificial tasks with visual feedback; the review elaborates design criteria per modality.
units_and_conditions: Qualitative; applies to feedback frequency and to physical guidance
locator: Salmoni: PubMed 6399752 (no abstract available); secondary: Marchal-Crespo & Reinkensmeyer 2009, section 'Assistive controllers'; Sigrist: abstract, PubMed 23132605
limitations: Primary texts not accessed (Springer/APA login); Salmoni reviewed knowledge-of-results feedback, not physical or ink-level guidance; Sigrist's detailed moderators (task complexity, skill) could not be verified
relevance_to_design: Frames the central risk: an always-on correcting nib improves the written trace but can reduce what the writer learns
transferability_reason: The theory is modality-general and the nib acts as concurrent outcome guidance, but no reviewed work concerns an ungrounded ink-displacing tool
design_implication: Treat correction as a performance aid by default; in any learning mode schedule unassisted trials, fade help, and judge success only by unassisted retention/transfer

citation: Winstein CJ, Pohl PS, Lewthwaite R (1994) Effects of physical guidance and knowledge of results on motor learning: support for the guidance hypothesis. Res Q Exerc Sport 65(4):316-323
task_or_setup: Movements to a target; 2x2 design crossing feedback form (physical guidance vs knowledge of results) with relative frequency (high vs faded); retention and transfer tests
participants_or_bench: Healthy subjects; N not stated in abstract
comparator: Knowledge of results vs physical guidance; high vs faded relative frequency
key_quantitative_findings: High-frequency physical guidance produced the poorest retention; both high-frequency feedback conditions produced the least accuracy in transfer (abstract). No effect sizes available.
units_and_conditions: Retention/transfer accuracy; exact metrics and delays not in abstract
locator: Abstract (PubMed 7886280); cited as guidance-hypothesis evidence in Reinkensmeyer & Patton 2009 (ref. 30) and Milot et al. 2010 (Introduction)
limitations: Abstract only; simple target movements; guidance moved the limb (not the ink); N and effect sizes unknown
relevance_to_design: Direct test that frequent physical guidance harms retention and that a faded schedule mitigates it
transferability_reason: Limb guidance vs ink displacement, but the shared mechanism (error removed during practice, reliance on the aid) applies
design_implication: Learning mode should use faded/reduced relative frequency of correction (assist-off blocks) rather than 100 % correction

citation: Marchal-Crespo L, Reinkensmeyer DJ (2009) Review of control strategies for robotic movement training after neurologic injury. J NeuroEng Rehabil 6:20
task_or_setup: Review of assistive (impedance, counterbalance, EMG, adaptive), challenge-based (incl. error amplification), haptic-simulation and coaching controllers
participants_or_bench: n/a (review of rehabilitation and healthy-subject studies)
key_quantitative_findings: Assist-as-needed ('faded guidance') is implemented with a deadband around the trajectory (no assistance inside), force/velocity-triggered assistance, compliance, or a forgetting factor; adaptive law P_i = f*P_(i-1) + g*e_i (P control parameter, e performance error); f = 1 gives no forgetting, 0 < f < 1 reduces assistance whenever error is small. Slacking: incomplete-SCI patients in a stiff impedance-controlled gait robot consumed 60 % less energy than in manually assisted therapy; post-stroke users of a compliant adaptive robot reduced their own force output. Guidance changes task dynamics so the task learned is not the target task. Error amplification (Patton et al.) produced straighter reaching after-effects; long-term benefit unknown.
units_and_conditions: Energy consumption (%); dimensionless adaptation parameters
locator: Sections 'Assistive controllers' (introduction; impedance-based assistance; performance-based adaptation, Eq. 1) and 'Challenge-based ... error-amplification strategies'
limitations: Mainly rehabilitation evidence; few controlled retention comparisons; 2009 state of the art
relevance_to_design: Supplies implementable assist-as-needed mechanics (deadband, forgetting factor) and the slacking risk
transferability_reason: Controllers were for grounded robots moving limbs, but the error-driven gain update with forgetting maps directly to a nib correction-gain schedule
design_implication: Make correction gain adaptive, e.g., gain_i = f*gain_(i-1) + k*error_i with f < 1 so help decays when the writer is accurate, plus a deadband so natural variability is not corrected (design proposal)

citation: Reinkensmeyer DJ, Patton JL (2009) Can robots help the learning of skilled actions? Exerc Sport Sci Rev 37(1):43-51; incl. Patton JL, Stoykov ME, Kovic M, Mussa-Ivaldi FA (2006) Evaluation of robotic training forces that either enhance or reduce error in chronic hemiparetic stroke survivors. Exp Brain Res 168:368-383 (abstract)
task_or_setup: Review of the authors' lab experiments: robot-guided trajectory learning (curve on a virtual sphere), steering with fixed vs adaptive guidance, force-field adaptation, error augmentation in stroke reaching
participants_or_bench: Trajectory study: 20 subjects, 126 demonstration and test movements; Patton 2006: 18 chronic stroke survivors, 834 movements, plus age-matched controls
comparator: Visual demonstration vs visual + haptic guidance; fixed vs adaptive (fading) guidance; error-enhancing vs error-reducing vs zero forces
key_quantitative_findings: Adding haptic guidance to visual demonstration gave no significant advantage (N = 20) and a nearly significant trend toward worse learning (Fig. 1). In steering, guidance groups performed better and the adaptive (fading) group showed no error increase when guidance was removed. Guidance 'obviates' learning of error-based corrections; the motor system 'slacks' when errors are small. Patton 2006: significant improvement only when training forces magnified the original errors, not when they reduced errors or were zero. Guidance proposed mainly to make practice less dangerous/discouraging (example given: a child with poor coordination learning to write).
units_and_conditions: Significance-level results; lab tasks
locator: Sections on the guidance hypothesis and steering; 'Using guidance to aid in dynamic adaptation' (Fig. 3); error augmentation (Fig. 4C); Fig. 1; Patton 2006 abstract (PubMed 16249912)
limitations: Review of own studies; lab tasks; stroke error-augmentation evidence is short-term after-effects; Patton 2006 abstract only
relevance_to_design: Explains the mechanism (reduced error signal) and gives two levers: performance-based fading and error augmentation
transferability_reason: Whole-arm robotic guidance, but the error-signal mechanism is modality independent and applies to nib correction that removes visible error
design_implication: Use correction mainly to keep novices/children motivated and out of large errors, fade it with performance, and for proficient users consider error augmentation on top of a small background of help

citation: Heuer H, Lüttgen J (2015) Robot assistance of motor learning: a neuro-cognitive perspective. Neurosci Biobehav Rev 56:222-240
task_or_setup: Review classifying learning tasks by products and mechanisms of learning and predicting effects of robot assistance
participants_or_bench: n/a (review)
comparator: Haptic guidance vs error-amplifying / divergent force fields across task classes
key_quantitative_findings: Robotic guidance facilitates learning of dynamic features of trajectories and impedes learning of kinematic and dynamic transformations; dynamic transformations can profit from error-amplifying forces; learning of spatial features of trajectories is impeded by haptic guidance but can be facilitated by divergent force fields; guidance may induce a passive role of the motor system (abstract).
units_and_conditions: Qualitative synthesis
locator: Abstract (PubMed 26192105)
limitations: Abstract only; no pooled effect sizes; force-based assistance only
relevance_to_design: Letter shape is a spatial trajectory feature, the class where guidance impedes learning; fluency/timing are dynamic features where it can help
transferability_reason: The task classification transfers to handwriting; the assistance modality (grounded forces) differs from ink displacement
design_implication: Do not rely on nib correction to teach letter shape; if shape learning is the goal, reveal or amplify errors; reserve guidance-like help for fluency/timing aims

citation: Milot M-H, Marchal-Crespo L, Green CS, Cramer SC, Reinkensmeyer DJ (2010) Comparison of error-amplification and haptic-guidance training techniques for learning of a timing-based motor task by healthy individuals. Exp Brain Res 201(2):119-131
task_or_setup: Pinball-like timing game (wrist movement to press a button at the right time); robot retarded/accelerated the movement from sensed initiation-timing error: haptic guidance (HG) reduced, error amplification (EA) increased errors (gain k changed by +/-90 %); 20 % catch trials with the manipulation removed; retention identical to baseline; generalization to untrained targets
participants_or_bench: 20 healthy right-handed adults (12 F, 8 M), 18-30 y (mean 24.0 +/- 2.7); within-subject, randomized order of EA and HG
comparator: Baseline (B3) vs retention after EA and after HG
key_quantitative_findings: Trained targets: EA 13 +/- 7 -> 10 +/- 6 ms (t(18) = 3.06, P = 0.015); HG 13 +/- 6 -> 12 +/- 6 ms (t(18) = 1.96, P = 0.035); no difference between techniques (P = 0.47). More skilled subgroup (n = 13, final k >= 0.1): EA improved retention by 4 +/- 3 ms (P = 0.002) vs HG 1 +/- 4 ms (P = 0.175), between conditions P = 0.015. Less skilled (n = 7): HG 2 +/- 2 ms (P = 0.02) vs EA -0.1 +/- 2 ms (P = 0.5), between P = 0.065.
units_and_conditions: Absolute timing error (ms), mean +/- SD; immediate retention
locator: Methods (Subjects; Fig. 2 protocol); Results pp. 124-126, Figs. 4-6
limitations: Timing, not spatial, task; small subgroups; immediate retention only; skill grouping confounded with EA magnitude (authors' caveat)
relevance_to_design: Best assistance depends on baseline skill: guidance for low skill, error amplification for higher skill
transferability_reason: Grounded wrist robot and timing task; skill dependence is plausibly general but letter learning is spatial
design_implication: Choose the mode per user skill (correction for beginners, error-revealing/amplifying for proficient users) and keep ~20 % assist-off catch strokes to maintain engagement and measure unassisted skill

citation: Williams CK, Tremblay L, Carnahan H (2016) It pays to go off-track: practicing with error-augmenting haptic feedback facilitates learning of a curve-tracing task. Front Psychol 7:2010
task_or_setup: Self-paced tracing of a sinusoidal curve with a Phantom Omni stylus (amplitude 155.6 mm, path 392.4 mm at the stylus; visual gain 1.48); 100 practice trials (20 blocks x 5). Error minimization (EM): spring toward curve outside a 0.8 mm deadband, 0.3 N/mm saturating at 1 N; error augmentation (EA): spring away, 0.3 N/mm saturating at 0.3 N. Tests without augmented feedback: immediate retention, ~1 day retention (M = 1.1 d), mirror-reversed transfer
participants_or_bench: 27 adults (24 F, 3 M; 22-55 y, M = 28.5), 9 per group (EM, EA, control)
key_quantitative_findings: Tracing error, group effect: immediate retention F(2,24) = 6.8, p = 0.005, partial eta^2 = 0.36; delayed retention F(2,24) = 4.9, p = 0.017, 0.29; transfer F(2,24) = 5.9, p = 0.008, 0.33. EM less accurate than EA at all three tests (p = 0.006, 0.016, 0.009) and than control at immediate retention (p = 0.021) and transfer (p = 0.042; Games-Howell p = 0.094). Acquisition: EA worst speed-accuracy cost (F(2,23) = 15.4, p < 0.001, 0.57). Speed-accuracy cost at tests: only immediate retention significant (F(2,24) = 4.0, p = 0.031, 0.25). Movement time no group differences (~13 s).
units_and_conditions: Tracing error (plotted, Fig. 7), ANOVA F, partial eta^2; forces on the hand via grounded device
locator: Methods: Apparatus, Task; Results: acquisition (Figs. 4-6), retention/transfer (Fig. 7); Discussion
limitations: Single simple curve; n = 9 per group; no pre-test; EA not better than control; grounded force feedback, not ink correction
relevance_to_design: Closest analogue to template tracing: error-minimising assistance with a sub-mm deadband left learners less accurate once removed, up to 1 day later
transferability_reason: Spatial path-tracing task like guided writing, but assistance acted on the hand, not on the trace
design_implication: In learning mode do not minimise visible error by default; an error-revealing (or augmenting) mode is at least as good as none; bound and fade any assistance

citation: Bluteau J, Coquillart S, Payan Y, Gentaz E (2008) Haptic guidance improves the visuo-manual tracking of trajectories. PLoS ONE 3(3):e1775
task_or_setup: PHANToM Omni stylus over a flat screen; Exp 1: 2 Arabic + 2 Japanese-inspired unfamiliar letters (20 test trials pre/post); Exp 2: ellipses, test shapes never trained. Three training sessions per participant (Latin square): position guidance HGP (PD spring pulling tip to the next trajectory point; 0.4 N/mm, 0.2 N.s/mm in Exp 1; 0.6 N/mm, 0.2 N.s/mm in Exp 2), force guidance HGF (expert force profile from a 0.1 kg model; PD 0.5 N/mm, 0.1 N.s/mm), no guidance NHG
participants_or_bench: Exp 1: 23 right-handed adults (18-26 y); Exp 2: 24 right-handed adults (18-28 y)
comparator: No-guidance training session; pre vs post tests without guidance in the same session
key_quantitative_findings: Exp 1: velocity-peak decrease only after HGF (session x period F(2,44) = 5.01, p < .05; e.g., letter 2: 9.42 -> 7.06 peaks; letter 4: 11.12 -> 8.86); mean velocity increased only after HGF (F(2,44) = 11.09, p < .05); no training effect on shape (DTW) for any mode (authors suggest ceiling effect). Exp 2 (untrained ellipses, mean +/- SE, Table 2): velocity peaks HGP 14.48 -> 10.19, HGF 14.19 -> 9.20 (both significant; NHG 11.36 -> 13.80), mode x test F(2,46) = 8.86; mean velocity HGF 4.62 -> 6.23 cm/s (significant; HGP 5.13 -> 5.88, NHG 5.66 -> 5.14), F(2,46) = 13.22; shape (DTW) no interaction, F(2,46) = 0.45.
units_and_conditions: Velocity peaks per trajectory, mean velocity (cm/s), DTW shape score; immediate post-test without guidance
locator: Methods (Exp 1 training sessions; Exp 2); Results Exp 1 (velocity peaks, mean velocity, shape matching) and Exp 2 with Table 2; Discussion
limitations: No delayed retention; three training sessions per participant (Latin square) with carry-over risk; adults; time-indexed playback guidance; stylus on a screen, not ink on paper
relevance_to_design: Handwriting-like evidence that guidance improves fluency (kinematics) but not shape, and that force-profile guidance beats position guidance
transferability_reason: Grounded device that moves the hand; the pen cannot apply net force to the hand, but the null effect of position correction on shape is directly relevant
design_implication: Do not expect nib correction to teach shape; if a cue for fluency is wanted, make it about timing/velocity (e.g., vibrotactile rhythm) rather than position

citation: Korres G, Park W, Eid M (2021) Contactless kinesthetic feedback to support handwriting using magnetic force. IEEE Trans Haptics (accepted manuscript)
task_or_setup: KATIB: 2-DOF parallel manipulator moves a permanent magnet under a touchscreen; stylus carries stacked neodymium magnets. Proactive (full) guidance: magnet leads point-to-point at maximum force; retroactive (partial): magnet activated only when stylus-to-target distance exceeds epsilon. Psychophysics: copy task of unfamiliar Arabic letters (5 difficulty levels), kinesthetic feedback randomly on/off, 10 s target duration
participants_or_bench: 16 adults (9 male, 24-39 y)
key_quantitative_findings: Maximum lateral force 0.43 N at 3.5 mm magnet-stylus offset; stylus tilt up to 40 deg from normal gives negligible lateral force; workspace 80 x 60 mm; unattended playback RMSE < 3 mm; copy RMSE significantly lower with feedback at all difficulty levels (t-test, p < 0.01); completion time closer to the 10 s target with feedback; ergonomics rating mean 59 % (0-100).
units_and_conditions: N, mm, RMSE (mm), s; guided (assisted) performance only
locator: Sec. 3 (Algorithms 1-2); Sec. 4.1 (Fig. 7); Sec. 4.2 (Fig. 8); Sec. 4.3 (Fig. 9); Sec. 5 (Figs. 10-12)
limitations: No retention test; only proactive guidance tested; epsilon not reported in extracted text; adults
relevance_to_design: Tip-level forces of ~0.4 N suffice to steer a lightly held stylus; tilt sensitivity and workspace limits matter; users valued free stylus control
transferability_reason: Grounded magnetic force at the tip vs ungrounded nib displacement; force levels and acceptance data still informative
design_implication: Error-triggered (retroactive) help maps to a deadband correction; measure retention separately from assisted accuracy

task_or_setup: Electromagnet (Intertec ITS-MS-5030-12VDC, 5 cm dia., 12 V, 11 W) on a bi-axial stepper stage (full step 0.2 mm, quarter-stepped) under a Sensel Morph tablet (6502 DPI, 500 Hz, 2 ms latency); ordinary paper; 3D-printed ballpoint pen with ring magnet; time-free model-predictive contouring control (horizon N = 10) pulls the pen back toward the path while the user sets the speed; if the pen is lifted the last known position is used (UIST version)
participants_or_bench: Exp A: 12 participants (open loop dePENd-like vs time-indexed MPC vs MPCC, one complex shape); Exp B: 12 participants (8 M, 4 F, 28.2 +/- 2.2 y), 6 shapes each drawn once with and once without guidance
key_quantitative_findings: Lateral force up to 488 mN at 11 W; positional dispersion 2.8 +/- 0.8 mm (300 repetitions, magnet full strength, passive pen); solve time 7.4 +/- 3.0 ms, pen-to-magnet latency ~10 ms, ~20 ms total. Exp A pen-to-path error OL 4.1 +/- 0.7, MPC 3.9 +/- 1.3, MPCC 2.0 +/- 0.6 mm (H(2) = 20.76, p < .001); pen-to-magnet 38.2 +/- 25.1 / 8.6 +/- 1.6 / 4.6 +/- 0.9 mm. Exp B mean error with vs without guidance: circle 2.19 vs 4.26, spiral 2.55 vs 4.38, sinusoid 2.53 vs 5.08, dog 2.31 vs 3.81, ellipse 2.40 vs 3.84 mm (ratio 0.50-0.62), line 1.18 vs 1.03 mm (n.s.); feedback main effect F = 46.187, p < .001; perceived force 3.50 +/- 0.86 (5-point). Corner cutting grows with curvature (simulation, Fig. 16). No learning/retention measured ('long-term learning ... beyond the scope').
units_and_conditions: mm (mean +/- SD), mN, ms, Likert 1-5; assisted performance
locator: arXiv v1: Sec. 4.1 p. 4; Secs. 6.3-6.4 p. 9; Sec. 7 and Table 2 pp. 9-10; Sec. 8 and Table 3 pp. 10-11; Table 4 p. 12; Secs. 10-11 p. 13; UIST'20 'Input and Output Devices'
limitations: Guided performance only; guided error ~2 mm is four times the pen's +/-0.5 mm range; slow stage limited drawing speed; grounded magnet under the tablet
relevance_to_design: Best evidence on closed-loop, time-free guidance that preserves agency; also quantifies unguided shape errors (3.8-5.1 mm) that exceed a +/-0.5 mm nib range
transferability_reason: Tip forces from ground vs ungrounded nib displacement; the control concepts (time-free progress variable, gentle pull-back) transfer fully
design_implication: Parameterise the target by a time-free progress variable along the path; pull back smoothly rather than snap; accept that the nib can only polish, not form, novice shapes

citation: Rivers A, Moyer IE, Durand F (2012) Position-correcting tools for 2D digital fabrication. ACM Trans Graph 31(4) (Proc. SIGGRAPH 2012)
task_or_setup: Handheld frame (~13 x 10 x 9 in) carrying a router, vinyl cutter or pen; frame camera tracks printed marker tape (image registration ~4 ms); two stepper-driven eccentrics move the tool within the frame; on-tool screen shows plan, tool position and correction-range circle
participants_or_bench: Authors' prototype; no formal user study
comparator: Manual positioning (pilot: users with an accurate location display kept the tool within 1/8 in of the plan)
key_quantitative_findings: Correction range set to twice the observed human error: users stayed within 1/8 in (3.2 mm) -> range radius 1/4 in (6.35 mm; 1/2 in circle); stage limited to ~95 % of eccentric range; 62 oz-in steppers prevented backdriving. Constant-speed mode: tool advances at 0.2 in/s (~5 mm/s) by default and stops at the range edge until the user catches up. Freeform mode: target = closest plan point to the range centre; 4 ranked candidate paths (walk along the border within range ... 'don't move'); user should not diverge faster than ~0.2 in/s. Pen plot of a 6 in pattern: mean error 0.009 in (0.23 mm), max 0.023 in (0.58 mm).
units_and_conditions: inch values converted to mm; in/s; ms
locator: PDF pages: Sec. 3.4 p. 3; Secs. 4-4.1 pp. 3-4; Secs. 4.2.1-4.2.2 and Fig. 5 pp. 4-5; Sec. 5.1 and Fig. 6 p. 5; Sec. 6 and Fig. 10 p. 6
limitations: Bench demonstrations only; frame rests on the workpiece (effectively grounded, large); no learning or user-performance statistics

transferability_reason: Same division of labour and bounded correction; differences are range (+/-0.5 mm vs +/-6.35 mm) and a hand-held, ungrounded pen body
design_implication: Size range from measured user error; show or cue remaining headroom; when out of range hold/stop rather than jump, prefer staying on the path over shortcuts, and re-acquire when the user returns

IEEE Trans Hum-Mach Syst 48(5):509-525; with Abbink DA, Mulder M, Boer ER (2012) Haptic shared control: smoothly shifting control authority? Cogn Tech Work 14:19-28 (not retrieved) and Mulder M, Abbink DA, Boer ER (2012) Sharing control with haptics. Hum Factors 54(5):786-798 (abstract)
task_or_setup: Definition, design axioms and domain reviews (automotive, surgery, brain-machine interfaces, learning) of shared control; Mulder 2012: fixed-base driving-simulator curve negotiation, manual vs haptic shared control vs automation
participants_or_bench: Mulder 2012: 42 drivers
key_quantitative_findings: Shared control: human and robot interact congruently in a perception-action cycle on a task either could do alone. Axiom 1: each agent directly perceives how its intent is shaped by the other; corollary: minimise conflicts by modelling robot actions on human behaviour and, in conflicts, ensure the human has time and ability to influence the robot. Level of haptic authority = stiffness around the controller's optimal steering angle (automotive example). Learning: fixed-gain guidance may be detrimental and shared control can de-skill; participants get annoyed when resisting forces contrary to their intentions. Mulder 2012 (abstract): vs manual, haptic shared control needed 16 % lower steering-wheel reversal rate and 15 % lower SD of wheel angle with 11 % lower peak lateral error; full automation gave 35 % lower peak lateral error but placed the human in a supervisory role.
units_and_conditions: % change vs manual (driving simulator)
locator: Abbink 2018 (UCL accepted-manuscript pagination) Secs. II.A-II.B (pp. 3-4), III.B (p. 6), VI and VI.A (pp. 9-10); Mulder 2012 abstract (PubMed 23156623)
limitations: Review; driving/surgery domains; Abbink 2012 text not accessed (Springer login); Mulder numbers from abstract
relevance_to_design: Vocabulary and rules for continuous authority sharing and override/conflict handling
transferability_reason: Principles are domain independent; torque-level sharing on a grounded interface differs from ungrounded nib displacement
design_implication: Expose correction authority as a continuous gain the user can feel and overrule; avoid sustained conflict by fading correction when the writer persistently deviates; keep the writer in the loop in learning mode

citation: Israr A, Choi S, Tan HZ (2006) Detection threshold and mechanical impedance of the hand in a pen-hold posture. Proc. IEEE/RSJ IROS 2006, 472-477
task_or_setup: B&K 4810 minishaker drives a PHANToM 1.0A stylus along its length (vibration mostly tangential to the skin); stylus held like a pen; elbow/forearm on an armrest; three-interval forced-choice adaptive thresholds (4 dB then 1 dB steps, 12 reversals) at 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 320, 500 Hz; 1 s bursts; accelerometer and Nano17 force sensor

Skin impedance roughly constant below 40 Hz at -36 to -38 dB re 1 N.s/mm (about 12.6-15.8 N.s/m; conversion by this ledger), then -7 dB/octave (40-80 Hz) and -16 dB/octave (80-160 Hz), flat 160-320 Hz, +16 dB/octave 320-500 Hz. Prior haptic experience no effect (F(1,406) = 0.49, p = 0.48). Brisben 1999 abstract adds: contact force 0.05-1.0 N had no effect on grasped-cylinder thresholds.

task_or_setup: Review of natural (visual, proprioceptive, tactile) and supplementary (visual, haptic, auditory) feedback in handwriting control and learning
participants_or_bench: n/a (review; Table 1 lists vision studies)
comparator: Vision vs no vision; delayed vision; supplementary feedback modalities
key_quantitative_findings: Vision mainly serves topocinetic (layout) control and stroke-repetition monitoring. Tamada (1995), 8 adults: visual-feedback delays of 0, 33, 67, 100, 133, 167, 267 and 500 ms increased writing error rate with delay, especially stroke repetitions (e.g., 'feeeling'). Smyth & Silvers (1987), 12 adults: word orientation affected by loss of vision. Supplementary concurrent visual feedback slows and disrupts fluency (Portier & van Galen 1992), so visual feedback should come after, not during, movement. Haptic guidance needs an a-priori 'ideal' trajectory, questionable given individual handwriting variability; auditory feedback recommended for real-time kinematics.
